idiom_name: variadic configuration functions applied over documented defaults
implementation_notes: Language-neutral blueprint: declare an option type whose values are functions from the (unexported) configuration target to nothing; provide one exported constructor per setting that closes over the caller's value and returns such a function; let the public constructor take a variadic option list, install documented defaults on a fresh target, apply every option in the order given, then validate and publish the object. Keep the target unexported so no caller can retain or mutate it, document 'later option wins' plus any mutually exclusive combination, and give options that can fail a way to report the error (a wider option type or a final validation step). Reusable option groups are ordinary option lists applied in the same pass. Where the language has named or default parameters, the same contract is expressed by the signature itself and the machinery is unnecessary.
code_sketch:
Option      := function(Config) -> void          # one setting each
WithTimeout := |d| -> Option { c => c.timeout = d }

New(required, options...):
    cfg = defaults()                    # documented non-zero defaults
    for o in options: o(cfg)            # applied in call order
    validate(cfg)                       # fail fast before publishing
    return Server(cfg)
pitfalls: Applying options to a shared or retained configuration value instead of a fresh per-construction target, so two constructions end up sharing state.
Handing the configuration object back to callers (or accepting it after construction), which lets defaults be bypassed and a published object be mutated.
No documented precedence for repeated options and no conflict check for mutually exclusive ones, so the failure appears as a mysterious runtime configuration instead of an error at construction time.
Options that close over mutable external state and mutate it as a side effect, making call order significant and test behaviour non-deterministic.

Failure to validate the assembled configuration before publishing the target, so an object with an impossible combination (TLS enabled with InsecureSkipVerify) exists briefly before failing on first use.
Using a single Option interface{} or any type to represent all options, losing static type safety and making it impossible for the compiler to detect options applied to the wrong target type.
Options that embed resources requiring cleanup (handles, connections) but never transfer ownership, so the caller cannot know when the target releases them.

New options added with changed defaults to existing released APIs, silently changing behaviour for callers who did not specify that option — always make new options additive and document default changes in release notes.

Wrong move: use functional options as the wire format for YAML/JSON or control-plane configuration -> opaque closures cannot be serialized, diffed, or validated before construction fails -> instead parse into a typed options struct and translate it into options at the boundary.

Wrong move: apply reusable options that capture request-scoped tokens or trace IDs -> the values persist on every object built from that option and can leak across requests -> instead pass request data through context or method parameters and reserve options for construction wiring.

Wrong move: rely on option order without documenting overwrite or composition semantics -> repeated settings silently replace or wrap one another and behavior changes when callers reorder them -> instead define precedence and reject incompatible combinations during construction.
